\section[bolṇe]{\mr{बोलणे} (bolṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C05-bolne}



\begin{quote}
Until now, verbs of \emph{being} and \emph{meeting}. Here is your first verb of \textbf{doing} — to speak — and the pattern that runs every Marathi verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{बो}} (\emph{bo}) + \textbf{\mr{ल}} (\emph{la}) + \textbf{\mr{णे}} (\emph{ṇe}, the \textbf{retroflex} \mr{ण} \emph{ṇa} with the \emph{-e} stroke) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{बोलणे}} \emph{bolṇe}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{बोलणे}} (\emph{bolṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}) is a native Indo-Aryan verb on the stem \textbf{bol-} — the same \emph{bol-} as Hindi \emph{bolnā} and Punjabi \emph{bolṇā}. Its ending \textbf{-\mr{णे}} (\emph{-ṇe}) is the Marathi \textbf{infinitive} (\textquotedblleft{}to \_\_\_\textquotedblright{}): \emph{bol-ṇe} \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} \emph{bheṭ-ṇe} \textquotedblleft{}to meet,\textquotedblright{} \emph{ye-ṇe} \textquotedblleft{}to come.\textquotedblright{} Strip \emph{-ṇe} and you have the stem to build on: \textbf{bol-}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem + gendered present ending}]
From the stem you build the present tense — and, as with \emph{yeto/yete}, it splits by the speaker's gender:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{बोलतो}} (\emph{mī bolto}) — a man speaks
  \item \textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{बोलते}} (\emph{mī bolte}) — a woman speaks
  \item (plural / respectful: \textbf{\mr{बोलतो} / \mr{बोलता}})
\end{itemize}

The verb still ends the sentence; the copula-less present tense is one word doing the work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bolṇe\textquotedblright{} — to speak; then the stem (\emph{bol-})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} for your own gender (\emph{mī bolto} / \emph{mī bolte})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Marathi infinitive ending, and how does the present split? (\emph{-ṇe}; the present ending changes with the speaker's gender — \emph{bolto} m. / \emph{bolte} f.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mī marāṭhī bolto]{\mr{मी} \mr{मराठी} \mr{बोलतो} (mī marāṭhī bolto) — \textquotedblleft{}I speak Marathi\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C05-mi-marathi-bolto}



\begin{quote}
Your first full action-sentence — and it names the language itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — the phrase, assembled}
\textbf{\mr{मी}} (\emph{mī}, I) + \textbf{\mr{मराठी}} (\emph{marāṭhī}, Marathi, the object) + \textbf{\mr{बोलतो}} (\emph{bolto}, speak) $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}I Marathi speak,\textquotedblright{} verb last.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item A woman says \textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मराठी} \mr{बोलते}} (\emph{mī marāṭhī bolte}).
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{मराठी}} (\emph{marāṭhī}) is \textquotedblleft{}{[}the language{]} of \textbf{\mr{महाराष्ट्र}} (\emph{Mahārāṣṭra})\textquotedblright{} — the \textquotedblleft{}great kingdom/realm,\textquotedblright{} \emph{mahā} (\textquotedblleft{}great,\textquotedblright{} cousin of Latin \emph{magnus} and English \emph{magnitude}) + \emph{rāṣṭra} (\textquotedblleft{}nation, realm\textquotedblright{}). The people are the \emph{Marāṭhā}, the land \emph{Mahārāṣṭra}, and the tongue \emph{marāṭhī} — all one root. It carries the same \textbf{retroflex} sounds you keep meeting: the \mr{ट} (\emph{ṭa}) of \emph{marāṭhī}, the \mr{ळ} of \emph{kāḷjī}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The present tense needs no separate \textquotedblleft{}am/do\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\mr{बोलतो}} alone says \textquotedblleft{}I speak.\textquotedblright{} Contrast Hindi, which adds a copula (\emph{maiṁ hindī boltā \textbf{hūṁ}}); Marathi folds the \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{} into the verb ending. Cleaner, and gendered.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mī marāṭhī bolto/bolte\textquotedblright{} — I speak Marathi
  \item the root of \emph{marāṭhī} (\emph{Mahārāṣṭra} = \textquotedblleft{}great realm\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the name \emph{marāṭhī} come from? (\emph{Mahārāṣṭra}, \textquotedblleft{}great realm\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mahā} \textquotedblleft{}great\textquotedblright{} + \emph{rāṣṭra} \textquotedblleft{}nation.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rāhṇe]{\mr{राहणे} (rāhṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to live, to stay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C05-rahne}



\begin{quote}
A second verb on the same engine — \textbf{to live} — and a first postposition to place yourself somewhere.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{रा}} (\emph{rā}) + \textbf{\mr{ह}} (\emph{ha}) + \textbf{\mr{णे}} (\emph{ṇe}, retroflex) $\to$ \textbf{\mr{राहणे}} \emph{rāhṇe}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{राहणे}} (\emph{rāhṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to live, remain, stay\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{रह्}} (\emph{rah-}, \textquotedblleft{}to remain\textquotedblright{}) — the same root behind Hindi \emph{rahnā}. Present tense, gendered as always: \textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{पुण्यात} \mr{राहतो}} (\emph{mī puṇyāt rāhto}, a man) / \textbf{\mr{राहते}} (\emph{rāhte}, a woman) — \textquotedblleft{}I live in Pune.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} comes \emph{after} the noun}]
Look at \textbf{\mr{पुण्यात}} (\emph{puṇyāt}) = \textbf{\mr{पुणे}} (\emph{Puṇe}, the city) + \textbf{-\mr{ात}} (\emph{-āt}, \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}). Marathi glues \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} onto the \textbf{end} of the noun — a \textbf{post}position, not a preposition. Verb last, place-marker on the noun's tail: \emph{mī puṇyāt rāhto}, \textquotedblleft{}I in-Pune live.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rāhṇe\textquotedblright{} — to live; then \textquotedblleft{}mī puṇyāt rāhto/rāhte\textquotedblright{}
  \item how \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} attaches (\emph{Puṇe} + \emph{-āt} $\to$ \emph{puṇyāt})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} go in Marathi, and on what root is \emph{rāhṇe}? (On the \textbf{end} of the noun (\emph{-āt}); Sanskrit \emph{rah-} \textquotedblleft{}to remain.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kām karṇe]{\mr{काम} \mr{करणे} (kām karṇe) — \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C05-kaam-karne}



\begin{quote}
Your third verb — \textbf{to work} — and it closes a circle back to Chapter 1's greeting.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\mr{काम}} (\emph{kām}): \textbf{\mr{का}} + \textbf{\mr{म}} (\emph{ma}). \textbf{\mr{करणे}} (\emph{karṇe}): \textbf{\mr{क}} (\emph{ka}) + \textbf{\mr{र}} (\emph{ra}) + \textbf{\mr{णे}} (\emph{ṇe}, retroflex).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{करणे}} (\emph{karṇe}, \textquotedblleft{}to do, make\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{√\mr{कृ}} (\emph{kṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}), from PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}er-}. That is the very root hiding inside Chapter 1's \textbf{\mr{नमस्कार}} (\emph{namaskār} = \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{making} of a bow\textquotedblright{}) and inside \textbf{\mr{कर्म}} (\emph{karma}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing \textbf{done}\textquotedblright{}). And \textbf{\mr{काम}} (\emph{kām}, \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{}) is itself worn down from that same \textbf{\mr{कर्म}} (\emph{karma}). So \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{} is literally built twice from \emph{doing}: \textbf{\mr{काम} \mr{करणे}} (\emph{kām karṇe}) = \textquotedblleft{}work-do.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: noun + \mr{करणे} makes a verb}]
Marathi builds countless verbs as \textbf{noun + \mr{करणे}}: \emph{kām karṇe} (to work), \emph{madat karṇe} (to help), \emph{sevā karṇe} (to serve). Present tense, gendered: \textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{काम} \mr{करतो}} (\emph{mī kām karto}, m.) / \textbf{\mr{करते}} (\emph{karte}, f.) — \textquotedblleft{}I work.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kām karṇe\textquotedblright{} — to work; then \textquotedblleft{}mī kām karto/karte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root it shares with \emph{namaskār} and \emph{karma} (\emph{√kṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What links \emph{karṇe}, \emph{namaskār}, and \emph{karma}? (All from \emph{√kṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{} — and \emph{kām} \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{} is worn-down \emph{karma}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 12 recap — the first verbs}

\label{lesson:MR-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
Three verbs, one engine — sentences about yourself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — sentences about yourself}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Marathi} & \textbf{Say it} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\mr{मी} \mr{मराठी} \mr{बोलतो} / \mr{बोलते}. & \emph{mī marāṭhī bolto / bolte.} & I speak Marathi. \\
\mr{मी} \mr{पुण्यात} \mr{राहतो} / \mr{राहते}. & \emph{mī puṇyāt rāhto / rāhte.} & I live in Pune. \\
\mr{मी} \mr{काम} \mr{करतो} / \mr{करते}. & \emph{mī kām karto / karte.} & I work. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — the engine, in one look}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Infinitive} ends in \textbf{-\mr{णे}} (\emph{-ṇe}): \emph{bolṇe, rāhṇe, karṇe}.
  \item \textbf{Present} = stem + a \textbf{gendered} ending — \emph{-to} (m.) / \emph{-te} (f.): \emph{bolto/ bolte, rāhto/rāhte, karto/karte}. No separate \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{} — the ending carries it.
  \item \textbf{Verb goes last}; \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}} attaches to the noun's end (\emph{puṇyāt}).
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots banked}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{बोलणे}} (\emph{bolṇe}) — to speak (native \emph{bol-}).
  \item \textbf{\mr{मराठी}} (\emph{marāṭhī}) — from \emph{Mahārāṣṭra}, \textquotedblleft{}great realm.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\mr{राहणे}} (\emph{rāhṇe}) — to live (Sanskrit \emph{rah-}).
  \item \textbf{\mr{करणे}} (\emph{karṇe}) — to do/work (√\emph{kṛ} — root of \emph{namaskār}, \emph{karma}; \emph{kām} $\leftarrow$ \emph{karma}).
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all three sentences for your own gender
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak Marathi and I work\textquotedblright{} (\emph{mī marāṭhī bolto āṇi kām karto})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What three things does the Marathi present tense fold into one word? (The action, the person, and their gender — no separate \textquotedblleft{}am.\textquotedblright{}) From here, Marathi only opens further.
\end{tcolorbox}
